title: Moving backup and restore off Oracle's own tools
question: Tell me about a time you replaced a piece of working legacy infrastructure.

situation: I spent two years working on a mission-critical SWIFT application used to route international financial messages between banking institutions worldwide. Its backup and restore process relied on Oracle's native tooling.

Although the database tooling worked, it sat awkwardly inside a cross-platform application that had to behave consistently across several operating systems. It also meant that an important part of the application's data lifecycle was controlled outside the application itself.
task: I was tasked with replacing the Oracle-specific backup and restore path with a unified, application-driven migration framework, while keeping the system available and meeting the reliability and compliance requirements of a financial system.
The work had to fit into a large C++98 codebase with significant legacy complexity, alongside Java web services and an early multi-tenant architecture.
action: I designed and implemented an application-owned migration framework that replaced the Oracle-specific backup and restore mechanisms. This gave the application a consistent way to control and reason about its own migration lifecycle rather than delegating that behaviour to database-specific tooling.

The main challenge was extracting the migration logic from a legacy codebase where database operations had accumulated inside highly complex functions, some exceeding a thousand lines. I separated that logic into dedicated migration components with clearer responsibilities and interfaces.
Because the application had to behave consistently across multiple operating systems, I also had to account for platform-specific compilation and runtime behaviour throughout the migration path.
I validated the new implementation through extensive integration testing across the supported platforms and worked through the migration scenarios without interrupting the running system.
result: We replaced the Oracle-specific backup and restore path with an application-controlled migration framework while maintaining 100% system uptime and the required compliance standards for international financial data.

challenge: The biggest challenge was making a fundamental change to a data path that could not afford to fail. The codebase was large, old and cross-platform, so even a seemingly isolated change could have unexpected consequences in another operating system or part of the application.
hardestBug: The hardest part was not a single defect but validating the migration reliably across a complex multi-OS environment. Integration testing was largely manual, so verifying a migration meant exercising the complete flow on each supported platform. That experience made me realise how much confidence and engineering time could be gained by automating those scenarios.
differently: I would invest in automated cross-platform integration testing earlier. At the time, validating the migration required a significant amount of manual testing on each operating system, which made changes slower to verify and increased the cost of iteration.
aboutYourself: I learned that I enjoy taking something that works but has accumulated too much complexity and understanding it deeply enough to separate the essential behaviour from the historical implementation. The work reinforced that I am most engaged when there is a difficult architectural problem hidden inside an apparently simple change.
enjoyed: I enjoyed the process of taking large, tightly coupled legacy functions and gradually turning them into smaller, focused migration components. Seeing a difficult piece of infrastructure become something the application could own and reason about was particularly satisfying.
